deck.title: French Syllable and Stress
deck.sub: How a French word is divided and where the beat falls

panels.h: The French syllable. A French syllable has one sounded vowel. Several written letters often make one vowel sound: eau, ou, and ai are each one vowel, so beau is one syllable and maison is two, mai-son. A final e that is not sounded, the mute e (e muet), does not make a syllable in ordinary speech, so table is one syllable when it is spoken. In verse the mute e is counted before a consonant and not before a vowel.

q.prompt: How many syllables does maison have?
q.explain: Ai is one vowel sound and on another, so the word is mai-son, two syllables.

panels.h: Elision and liaison. A few short words drop their final vowel before a word that begins with a vowel or a mute h, and the spelling shows the loss: l’homme, j’ai, qu’il. This is elision. A final consonant that is silent before a pause is often sounded before a vowel and joined to it: in les amis the s is sounded as z. This is liaison. A word that begins with an aspirated h, such as héros, allows neither: le héros, les héros with no z.

q.prompt: Why is le homme written l’homme?
options: The e of le is elided before the mute h
The h is sounded, and so the article changes
q.explain: The h of homme is mute, so the word begins with a vowel sound, and le loses its e: l’homme.

panels.h: French stress. French does not stress a fixed syllable of the word, as Latin does. The beat falls on the last sounded syllable of the rhythmic group, which is often the end of a phrase rather than of each word. Parler, said alone, is stressed on -ler, but in parler au roi the beat falls on roi. So there is no penult to measure, as there is in Latin.

options: On the last sounded syllable of the group
On the first syllable of the stem
On the penult if it is long
On the syllable with an accent mark
q.explain: The group, not the word, takes the beat. Latin measures the penult, German stresses the stem, and French puts the beat at the end of the group.

panels.h: The accent marks are not stress. The written accents of French do not mark the beat. The acute in été marks a closed e, and the grave in mère an open one; the grave on à and où tells these words from a and ou. The circumflex often stands where an s was once written, as in forêt beside English “forest.”

q.prompt: What does the acute accent in été show?
options: The quality of the vowel, a closed e
That a letter has been lost
q.explain: French accent marks show the quality of a vowel or tell words apart, and they do not mark the stress.

exercise.title: French Syllable and Stress
exercise.desc: A short set on the French syllable: counting syllables, the mute e, elision and liaison, the stress of the group, and the accent marks.

items.q: How many syllables does this word have?
items.why: Ai is one vowel sound and on another: mai-son.

items.q: How many syllables does this word have?
items.why: Eau is one vowel sound, so beau is one syllable.

items.q: How many syllables does this word have in ordinary speech?
items.why: The final mute e is not sounded in ordinary speech, so table is one syllable.

items.q: How many syllables does this word have?
items.why: The word is u-ni-ver-si-té, with five sounded vowels.

items.q: How many syllables does this word have?
items.why: The word is par-lons, and the final s is not sounded.

items.q: Where does the stress fall in this word, said alone?
items.why: French stresses the last sounded syllable of the group, and a word said alone is a group by itself.

items.q: In this group, which word carries the beat?
items.why: The beat falls at the end of the rhythmic group, here on the last syllable of garçon.

items.a: A final vowel dropped before a vowel, and marked with an apostrophe
ds: A final consonant sounded before a vowel
The stress at the end of a group
items.why: In l’homme and j’ai the final vowel of le and je is dropped, and the apostrophe marks its place.

items.q: In les amis, how is the s of les pronounced?
items.why: This is liaison: the final consonant, silent before a pause, is sounded before a vowel, and an s is sounded as z.

items.q: Why do we write le héros and not l’héros?
items.a: The h of héros is aspirated, and it allows no elision
ds: The h of héros is mute
items.why: An aspirated h, though it is not pronounced, blocks both elision and liaison: le héros, les héros.

items.q: How many syllables does this word have in ordinary speech?
items.why: The middle e is mute and usually not sounded in ordinary speech: sam-di.

items.q: What does the circumflex in forêt often mark?
items.a: An s that was once written after the vowel
items.why: Compare English forest: the circumflex often stands where an older s has dropped out.

items.q: What does the grave accent on à show?
items.a: That it is the preposition, not a, the form of avoir
items.why: The grave on à and où tells these words apart from a and ou. It does not mark stress.

items.q: In verse, when is a mute e at the end of a word counted as a syllable?
items.a: Before a word that begins with a consonant
ds: Before a word that begins with a vowel
Only at the end of the line
items.why: In French verse the mute e is counted before a consonant and elided before a vowel; at the end of the line it is not counted.
